body:
in History |   	October 12th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

In 2002, the retired British sub­ma­rine lieu­tenant-com­man­der turned ama­teur his­to­ri­an Gavin Men­zies cre­at­ed a stir with a book about Chi­nese sea­far­ing in the fif­teenth cen­tu­ry. 1421: The Year Chi­na Dis­cov­ered the World (telling­ly titled 1421: The Year Chi­na Dis­cov­ered Amer­i­ca in the Unit­ed States) began as a glob­al his­to­ry of that year, only com­ing to focus on the claim of the title through the inter­ven­tions of pub­lish­ing-indus­try pro­fes­sion­als. They no doubt sensed a lucra­tive con­tro­ver­sy in the off­ing, and events proved them right. Not only did the book turn best­seller, it also man­aged the rare feat of draw­ing, among oth­er respons­es, a two-hour PBS doc­u­men­tary ded­i­cat­ed to debunk­ing it. Today, 1421 is most char­i­ta­bly remem­bered as a work of his­tor­i­cal fic­tion writ­ten around the idea that, even if Chi­na did­n’t actu­al­ly dis­cov­er the world, would­n’t it be neat if it had?
That ques­tion is hard­ly as friv­o­lous as it may sound. Much of Men­zies’ book has to do with the exploits of Zheng He, a Ming-dynasty admi­ral and diplo­mat whose fleet real­ly did make voy­ages to much of the world, or at least the parts sur­round­ing the Indi­an Ocean. Even if the claim that he beat Christo­pher Colum­bus to the Amer­i­c­as can’t be sup­port­ed, he real­ly did get around, and in seri­ous­ly impres­sive ships at that. In the Hoog video above, you can see Zheng He’s sto­ry told with retro 3D video-game graph­ics suit­able to con­vey the kind of adven­ture his life became. Yet it could hard­ly have begun more humbly: born into a Mus­lim fam­i­ly in the south­ern, Mon­gol-con­trolled Yun­nan province, he was cap­tured by the Ming mil­i­tary and cas­trat­ed in ado­les­cence. Harsh though that sounds, it made him able to accrue a kind of pow­er that could nev­er have been his oth­er­wise.
“The Ming empire was built on eunuchs,” says the video’s nar­ra­tor. “Unlike oth­er impe­r­i­al Chi­nese dynas­ties, the Ming ele­vat­ed cas­trat­ed men beyond what any had known.” Their inabil­i­ty to repro­duce and serve their own blood­line inspired the trust of the rulers: “What they lost in muti­la­tion, they gained in access to pow­er.” Under Zhu Di, known as the Yon­gle Emper­or, Zheng He became “the most pow­er­ful eunuch in the Ming Dynasty.” In order to project his pow­er over­seas, the emper­or decid­ed to con­struct “the great­est fleet the world has ever seen,” con­sist­ing of 300 trans­port ships, 180 war­ships, 240 sup­ply ships, 700 horse ships, and 36 mas­sive “trea­sure ships” that might have been the largest wood­en ves­sels ever to set sail. To lead this “mov­ing empire” with its staff of 27,000 — many of them eunuchs — he knew no one more reli­able than his old friend Zheng He.
This fleet’s expe­di­tions main­tained suf­fi­cient hege­mo­ny to ensure a peri­od of region­al sta­bil­i­ty some call the Pax Ming. At the same time, the civ­il ser­vice grew ever more resent­ful of the priv­i­leged eunuch class, and a light­ning strike on the For­bid­den City in 1421 was tak­en as a sign that the time had come to crit­i­cize their lead­er­ship. It would seem that Zhu Gaochi, the Yon­gle Emper­or’s son, took this crit­i­cism to heart. When he took pow­er as the Hongxi Emper­or after his father died while Zheng He was at sea, he put an end to the cost­ly naval expe­di­tions that could, in the­o­ry, one day have reached the New World. Ques­tions about why Chi­na’s age of mar­itime explo­ration had to end have more recent­ly been joined by oth­ers about whether such a vast fleet real­ly could have sailed, and for that mat­ter, whether the enor­mous trea­sure ships could even have been built in the first place. Chi­na may have done away with the eunuch sys­tem more than a cen­tu­ry ago, but there’s no doubt that its cur­rent lead­er­ship rec­og­nizes the impor­tance of sea pow­er — or that it has its eyes on the heav­ens.

Based in Seoul, Col­in Marshall writes and broad­casts on cities, lan­guage, and cul­ture. He’s the author of the newslet­ter Books on Cities as well as the books 한국 요약 금지 (No Sum­ma­riz­ing Korea) and Kore­an Newtro. Fol­low him on the social net­work for­mer­ly known as Twit­ter at @colinmarshall.

title: A 900-Page Pre-Pantone Guide to Color from 1692: A Complete High-Resolution Digital Scan
description:
in Art |   	October 12th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
There’s ahead of its time, then there’s Traité des couleurs ser­vant à la pein­ture à l’eau —
body:
in Art |   	October 12th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
There’s ahead of its time, then there’s Traité des couleurs ser­vant à la pein­ture à l’eau — or, in its orig­i­nal Dutch title, Klaer Ligh­t­ende Spiegel der Ver­fkon­st, a 900-page book of paint col­ors made before any such things were com­mon tools of the artist’s, scientist’s, and indus­tri­al designer’s trade. Author and artist A. Boogert cre­at­ed one, and only one, copy of his extra­or­di­nary man­u­al on col­or mix­ing in 1692. Appear­ing on the thresh­old of mod­ern col­or the­o­ry, and fea­tur­ing over 700 pages of col­or swatch­es, the book draws on Aristotle’s sys­tem of col­or rather than the new under­stand­ing of the col­or spec­trum, ful­ly elab­o­rat­ed by New­ton in his Opticks over a decade lat­er.
It would be anoth­er hun­dred years before a flood tide of col­or books began to make the the­o­ry more prac­ti­cal: from Goethe’s 1810 The­o­ry of Col­ors and Werner’s 1814 Nomen­cla­ture of Colour to the dream of col­or stan­dard­iza­tion real­ized: the Pan­tone com­pa­ny, launched in 1963.
But if A. Boogert had much influ­ence on the the­o­ry or prac­ti­cal appli­ca­tion of col­or in his day, there doesn’t seem to be much evi­dence for it. Of course most of the Dutch mas­ters had died when the book was com­plet­ed, and it seems unlike­ly that those still work­ing in 1692 would have been famil­iar with its sin­gle copy.

Instead, the book was meant to edu­cate water­col­orists, hence its French title, which refers to “water-based paint.” (A lit­er­al trans­la­tion of the Dutch runs some­thing like “clear­ly light­ing mir­ror of the paint­ing art.”) Medieval his­to­ri­an Erik Kwakkel found the book in a French data­base, “and it turns out to be quite spe­cial,” he writes, “because it pro­vides an unusu­al peek into the work­shop of 17th-cen­tu­ry painters and illus­tra­tors.

In over 700 pages of hand­writ­ten Dutch, the author, who iden­ti­fies him­self as A. Boogert, describes how to make water­colour paints. He explains how to mix the colours and how to change their tone by adding ‘one, two or three por­tions of water.’… In the 17th Cen­tu­ry, an age known as the Gold­en Age of Dutch Paint­ing, this man­u­al would have hit the right spot.”

The book is cur­rent­ly housed at Bib­lio­thèque Méjanes in Aix-en-Provence, where you’ll find full-page, zoomable, hi-res­o­lu­tion scans. “Beyond being infor­ma­tion­al, the images from the book are stun­ning and addic­tive flip through,” notes Refinery29. “They resem­ble page after page of Pan­tone col­or chips, except with­out the house­hold name.” One won­ders if “A. Boogert” would have become a house­hold name had his book been print­ed and dis­trib­uted. But his col­or sys­tem was already pass­ing away in the New­ton­ian age of col­or spec­trums and wheels, until paint chips final­ly came back in style. Vis­it the col­or man­u­al online here.

Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2019.
Relat­ed Con­tent: 
Goethe’s Col­or­ful & Abstract Illus­tra­tions for His 1810 Trea­tise, The­o­ry of Col­ors: Scans of the First Edi­tion
Werner’s Nomen­cla­ture of Colour, the 19th-Cen­tu­ry “Col­or Dic­tio­nary” Used by Charles Dar­win (1814)
The Vibrant Col­or Wheels Designed by Goethe, New­ton & Oth­er The­o­rists of Col­or (1665–1810)
Josh Jones is a writer and musi­cian based in Durham, NC.

title: A Little Fantasy Goes a Long Way
description:
Pocket Review
                In this photography exhibition, works vacillate between intimacy and unknowability, like a fractur
body:
Pocket Review
                In this photography exhibition, works vacillate between intimacy and unknowability, like a fractured peep show. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Janice Guy "Untitled" (1977, printed 2026), eight silver gelatin prints (all images Julia Curl/Hyperallergic)
    
        
            “Abandon the search for Truth; settle for a good fantasy.” These words, taken from Fran Lebowitz and written on the wall to warn all ye who enter Luhring Augustine’s Chelsea gallery, set up the premise for its current group show: settle for a good fantasy.It’s an admittedly juicy quotation. So juicy, indeed, that the gallery has hung Shaun Pierson’s photograph of a very voluptuous strawberry — seriously, it’s like the Venus of Willendorf of strawberries — right next to it, as if to underscore the point: Photography is always chasing a fantasy.Shaun Pierson, "Untitled (Strawberry on Lace)" (2026), archival pigment printThe exhibition’s main room leans into this, showing portraiture's fragmentary, erotic side. Works by Pierson, David Seider, and Janice Guy vacillate between intimacy and unknowability, like a fractured peep show. Curved, freckled backs touch. Beautiful shards of women’s faces are pieced together, seemingly pulled from the dark. Guy’s grids of self-portraits from the 1970s are particularly arresting, and not just because she also happens to be beautiful.

title: When the Accessibility Conveyor Belt Jams
description:
Pocket Review
								A malfunction in Finnegan Shannon’s installation at Pioneer Works led to new insights.
body:
Pocket Review
								A malfunction in Finnegan Shannon’s installation at Pioneer Works led to new insights.
						
								
																
														
								
						
		
	  		    
        
            Installation view of There's no me without you at Pioneer Works (photo Bryan Martin/Hyperallergic)
    
		
				
						Finnegan Shannon’s There's no me without you at Pioneer Works considers the fragility of systems and the consequences of their breakdown for disabled bodies. The installation is a 12-foot-long square conveyor belt — think conveyor-belt sushi — in a maroon-carpeted room that carries and displays objects for visitors to interact with, from plush chairs to open spaces for individuals who can’t access the seating. Masks, accessible text, hand sanitizer, DIY air purifiers, and descriptive audio are also available, defining Shannon’s vision for an equitable, gentle engagement with art.Three artists will be presented during the show’s run. For the first month, Ariana Martinez places small objects in dishes atop the moving presentation for visitors to pick up and touch. These small, tactile, fidget-like objects range from ceramic strips to masses of rope, all of which delight. Installation views of There's no me without you at Pioneer Works (photo Bryan Martin/Hyperallergic)Unfortunately, during my visit, the conveyor belt wasn't turned on, which undermined the apparatus's accessibility intent. Staff eventually came up to switch it on, but when the machine proved stuck, they left without resolving the issue. The inert belt became a frustrating metaphor for institutions and a larger social apathy toward accessibility needs. Spurred by fellow visitors’ confusion, I gently rocked a jammed plate side to side to see if it would help, and the belt started moving. Although accidental, Shannon's intent crystallized. We are all interdependent. Creative solutions are inexorably linked to disability, making the subject ripe for artmaking. The installation’s deviation from what I expected, like disability itself, offered me a new perspective on the world — a reminder of our collective responsibility to those who live in it. There’s no me without you continues at Pioneer Works (159 Pioneer Street, Red Hook, Brooklyn) through December 20. The exhibition was organized by Pioneer Works. 
									
											
												Pocket Review
											
											
												Finnegan Shannon

title: A View From the Easel: Flor Khan
description:
Community
                “Here, I am allowed to play, to not know the answers, to let the message evolve on its own timing.”
body:
Community
                “Here, I am allowed to play, to not know the answers, to let the message evolve on its own timing.”
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            Welcome to the 358th installment of A View From the Easel, a series in which artists reflect on their workspace. This week, Flor Khan collapses time and tenderly revives the memories of her ancestors.Want to take part? Check out our submission guidelines and share a bit about your studio with us through this form! All mediums and workspaces are welcome, including your home studio.Flor Khan, Bronx, New York CityHow long have you been working in this space?I have been working out of this particular space since March; before then, I worked in a number of artist studios and my own apartment.Describe an average day in your studio.The average day at the studio starts around 4pm, following my daytime job. Typically, I work on two to three pieces at once: Something is usually developing color in my photo processing work station, another piece is drying on the work line, and the other piece is steeping in tannins. If I'm lucky, I get to work with my sewing machine when the fabrics have dried. Before beginning my work, I turn on my salt lamp and light a candle for the ancestors; I ask for their permission to bring their memories back to life. With each stitch, and each photo transfer, I am brought closer to their memory, whether that's working with Victorian-era postcards featuring my Indo-Caribbean aunties or tapping into the photo albums of my late father. For background music, NPR's Tiny Desk plays whichever artist is being featured for the week.How does the space affect your work?My studio is a sacred space. It is a blessing to be surrounded by works in progress, keeping me in the flow: The pieces and I are in continuous conversation with one another. If the rain comes, I nest myself in the dim light of the candle and find myself in another world, one where the colors of grief are allowed to float around me, where catharsis is not shied away from, where I am allowed to be slow, intentional, soft with myself and the imperfections of the creation process. Here, I am allowed to play, to not know the answers, to let the message evolve on its own timing.How do you interact with the environment outside your studio?Being apart of the Kreate Hub community has been a beautiful experience. The Bronx community has been so welcoming. The hallways are covered in art from my neighboring studios and it inspires us all to be in conversation with one another. Down the hall you can find small business: studios for makeup design, costume, and film production. My studiomate and partner is a muralist and painter. We often find ourselves spending late nights creating, dreaming of world where we get to co-create workshops for our community. In fact, in the next coming weeks, we will be hosting a mashup of our artistries: a cyanotype-painting workshop on New York City landscapes.What do you love about your studio?I love the silence in the late night. Because I'm away from the main road, there are less ambulances whirring in the background; instead, I hear the train in the distance, I hear the raindrops, the candle flickering. When I am here, I am able to lose myself in the creation process because I am away from the distractions of home and house responsibilities. I love that I can leave my pieces unfinished, unbothered, no need to pick up the mess because the space allows for the process to bloom on its own time.What do you wish were different?If I could have more space for my tannins, this would be excellent! Right now, my water basin is down the hall and the slop sink is necessary for washing out my photo processors. Because I work primarily with photo processing liquids, running water near my workspace would be a dream! But, for now, I am grateful for my humble beginnings.What is your favorite local museum?El Museo del Barrio is one of my favorite museums uptown, one because it is accessible for the artist communities I live near and two because it centers on the contributions of Latin American and Caribbean culture and history. Their recent exhibition Sophie Rivera: Double Exposures spoke to the many layers of identity women hold in the art world. I was particularly blown away by her gelatin prints of children portraits shot in the 1980s, showcasing the class systems and lives lives in New York City streets. Being able to go to museums near me that represent my own culture is a powerful, affirming experience. As a Xicana-Latina, I felt seen in her art.What is your favorite art material to work with?I am deeply moved by photography and alternative photographic processes. Working with images allows me to revisit memories of family and loved ones who have passed; image-making also allows me to reinterpret the image itself: I overlay meaning by working with cartography, sewing news images atop, or mending parts that feel untrue or not whole. In the case of working with 19th-century postcard images, I disrupt the colonial gaze and bring historical context and agency back to the women that were often eroticized through the camera, staged in front of backdrops that removed them from their truer lived lives. Alternative photographic process reveal layers of colors and shadows that all exist with a single image, bringing truth to the saying "a picture is worth more than a thousand words"; the difference here is that I, as the artist, get to rewrite them.
                  
                      
                        Community
                      
                      
                        A View From the Easel

title: NYC to Provide Free Art Supplies to Grantees
description:
News
                Winners of the city's recently doubled grant for artists can also enjoy unlimited supplies from Materials f
body:
News
                Winners of the city's recently doubled grant for artists can also enjoy unlimited supplies from Materials for the Arts. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            An MFTA staff member helps a teacher check out at "After Hours" program. (all photos Anna Lee/Hyperallergic)
    
        
            Materials for the Arts (MFTA) is launching a new free shopping program for artists who receive city-funded grants on October 19, nearly three weeks after Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the Department for Cultural Affairs (DCLA) announced that they are doubling grants for individual artists and small nonprofits in New York City. The new MFTA program functions as a free supply base for the selected artists, who can now receive up to $10,000 in city-funded grants, which had remained at a $5,000 cap for the last 20 years. The organization will open its 35,000-square-foot warehouse to artist grantees on the second Monday of every month (apart from federal holidays) from 3 pm to 6 pm, offering materials such as leather spools originally used to make airplane seats, tomes dedicated to the visual arts, and dinosaur masks. The first iteration of the program will take place on Monday, October 19.Teachers wait in line at the MFTA's warehouse.“By broadening our operations to offer shopping days directly targeting these art grantees, we can ensure that more artists, more changemakers, and more New Yorkers have access to our city program,” Tara Sansone, the executive director of MFTA, told Hyperallergic.

title: Finding Vermeer in Unexpected Places
description:
Book Review
                Artists, filmmakers, poets, and the art market itself still bear traces of the Dutch painter’s influ
body:
Book Review
                Artists, filmmakers, poets, and the art market itself still bear traces of the Dutch painter’s influence, writes historian Ruth Bernard Yeazell in “Vermeer’s Afterlives.”
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Left: Johannes Vermeer, "Woman in Blue" (c. 1663); right: Han van Meegeren, "Woman Reading Music" (c. 1940) (images courtesy Rijksmuseum)
    
        
            As strange as it may sound, Johannes Vermeer’s fame is a relatively recent phenomenon. The Dutch painter known for his exquisite, enigmatic interior scenes fell into obscurity shortly after he died deeply in debt at only 43 years old in 1675. Vermeer was barely a footnote in the annals of art history until the mid-19th century, when the Parisian critic Théophile Thoré rediscovered his work. “Here’s someone we don’t know in France, and who very much deserves to be known!” the writer proclaimed in 1866. Thoré was drawn to Vermeer for the same reason he still fascinates museumgoers today: His small selection of attributed paintings — some 35 to date — and still-hazy biography spark more questions than answers. But in the three and a half centuries since his death, Vermeer’s mysterious works have also inspired a wealth of visual art, cinema, poetry, and literature.Mary Cassatt once said that Edgar Degas's "Madame Théodore Gobillard (Yves Morisot, 1838–1893)" (1869) was "much in the style of a Vermeer and quite as interesting." (image courtesy the Metropolitan Museum of Art)These artistic echoes are the focus of scholar Ruth Bernard Yeazell’s Vermeer’s Afterlives (2026), a richly illustrated exploration of the artist’s enduring and remarkably widespread impact through a careful survey of works made in his mythologized shadow. From Danish painter Vilhelm Hammershøi’s hushed canvases to experimental 20th-century film and sensual contemporary verse, Yeazell meticulously catalogs and analyzes the Delft painter’s iconography — especially his recurring solitary female figures gently illuminated by daylight filtered through nearby windows — and persistent commitment to open-ended interpretation over a singular narrative.
